Happen.et: Adopted in the 18th century from German Low German, which may have borrowed it from Dutch. A Dutch verb happen (“to snap”) is attested from the 16th century on; all ultimately imitative of children's speech (Kindersprache), akin to (South) Proto-Slavic *xapati…

s: haptic (relating to the sense of touch)
haptisch.et: From Ancient Greek ἁπτικός (haptikós, “able to come in contact with”), from ἅπτω (háptō, “to touch”) + -ικός (-ikós, “suffix forming an adjective from a noun”).

s: hapax legomenon (a word occurring only once in a given corpus)
A concept, an idea of a genius.
Hapax Legomenon.et: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἅπαξ λεγόμενον (hápax legómenon, “(something) said only once”), from ἅπαξ (hápax, “once”) and λεγόμενον (legómenon), passive participle of λέγω (légō).

s: the piecemeal introduction of new technologies
bit by bit, in small bits, in a piecemeal fashion
to curtail fundamental rights bit by bit
to be scarce, insufficient, stagnant, problematic
Es hapert an Bewerbern mit Berufserfahrung.
There is a lack of applicants with professional experience.
Ich verstehe ganz gut Französisch, aber beim Sprechen hapert es.
I can understand French quite well, but speaking it is problematic.
hapern.et: Via German Low German (and probably already Middle Low German) from Middle Dutch or early modern Dutch haperen.

s: Du hast ja von meinem Salat nur so’n kleinen Happs genommen.
You’ve just taken a tiny little bite of the salad I made.
Happs.et: Variant of Happen with German Low German nominal -s.

happig.et: Originally, "greedy, excessive, difficult to swallow", 18th-century creation apparently from happ, imitative of the sound of snapping. Possibly borrowed from German Low German; compare Low German happen, happen (“to snap, to devour”). Related to German Happen …

s: happening (spontaneous or improvised event, especially one that involves audience participation)
Happening.et: Unadapted borrowing from English happening, from Middle English *happenynge, *happnynge.
